reader.summary: The week was consumed by the final stretch of Brazil's presidential runoff between incumbent Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, with the vote set for Sunday, October 25. The two candidates held two debates: an earlier one marked by sharp exchanges over corruption and living costs, and a final one that was calmer but still combative. Polls from Datafolha and Quaest showed them essentially tied, making the outcome highly uncertain. A major controversy erupted over Meta's alleged social-media bias: Lula's campaign filed to disqualify Bolsonaro, a court ordered Meta to prove equal treatment within 24 hours, and the UN suggested Meta had disproportionately suppressed Lula's posts. Both campaigns made costly promises including free bus rides and cash-back schemes, and Lula fast-tracked welfare payments days before the vote. Markets hedged heavily ahead of the result. Inflation data presented a contradiction, with one report saying it undershot forecasts and another saying it breached the target. Prudential sold its Brazil and Mexico units for four billion dollars. A Newcastle disease outbreak threatened poultry exports. A court ordered the government to provide transportation for Indigenous voters in the Amazon. Foreign diplomats prepared for quick recognition of the winner, and Brazil accused Argentina's Milei of election meddling.

key_events.event: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro held their final presidential debate, clashing on living costs and corruption while striking a calmer tone than their first debate.
A Brazilian court ordered Meta to prove within 24 hours that it treated Lula and Bolsonaro campaigns equally after the UN suggested Meta disproportionately curbed Lula's posts.
Datafolha and Quaest polls showed Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied or within margin of error ahead of the Sunday runoff.
Lula fast-tracked welfare payments and opened the state toolbox with free bus rides and cash-back promises to woo undecided voters.
Prudential Financial sold its Brazil and Mexico insurance units to CNP Assurances for four billion dollars.
A Newcastle disease outbreak was detected at a turkey farm and at a supplier to major poultry company MBRF, raising export concerns.
Brazil's Supreme Court suspended the permit for a major Amazon gold mine.
A court ordered the government to provide transportation for Indigenous voters in the Amazon ahead of the runoff.
Brazil accused Argentina's President Milei of election meddling after he called Lula a thief ahead of the vote.

The Meta social media dispute will also get resolved. A court gave Meta 24 hours to prove it treated both candidates equally. Whatever the court decides, the losing side is likely to use it as an excuse to challenge the result in front of the Supreme Court.

Markets have been playing it safe because the race was so close. Once the vote is over, the real and the stock index will move sharply, and all those hedges traders built up will get unwound.

The free bus rides and cash-back promises that both candidates made will stop being a who's-courting-whom story and become either the winner's actual policy or a footnote.

The surprise to watch for: the losing campaign files a legal challenge right after the vote, citing the Meta ruling, and the Supreme Court has to step in before foreign governments can officially recognize the winner.
